title: I gave an AI $1,000 of real money to invest. Now I’m going to put it against a second AI.
author: mycapitallab
selftext:
I started a small experiment this week: I gave an AI agent I call Atlas $1,000 of real money and a conservative investing mandate.

Day 1: **$1,000 → $1,003.28**

Obviously +$3.28 proves absolutely nothing. The interesting part for me is what happens over time.

Next week I'm giving a second AI agent, Maverick, its own $1,000 — but with a much more aggressive mandate.

Same starting capital. Different risk rules. Real money.

I'm planning to track total return, drawdown, volatility, trading frequency and how each agent behaves when positions move against it.

I’ll keep the accounts separate so the results don't get mixed together.

**What else would you track to make Atlas vs. Maverick a meaningful comparison?**

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Because Atlas and Maverick have different mandates, raw return alone will mostly reveal which one took more exposure. I’d record daily gross and net exposure, largest position, turnover, fees, and return per unit of drawdown, then compare each agent with a simple benchmark matched to its risk level.

Also predefine what “conservative” and “aggressive” permit before Maverick starts, including leverage, concentration, and loss limits. Otherwise later rule changes could quietly reshape the $1,000-versus-$1,000 experiment. Will both agents receive market information on the same schedule and pay the same execution costs?

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
That’s an interesting experiment. I’ve been thinking about something similar, but I’m approaching it from the opposite direction.

I already have a refined trading bot, and the next step is to let an AI agent learn from its results — evaluating which decisions worked best, looking for patterns behind the edge, and trying to understand where the system could have behaved better.

In your case, I’d probably start by limiting both agents to the same small universe — maybe 10 pairs — so their decisions are easier to compare.

And one thing that could make the experiment even more interesting would be adding a **third agent that doesn’t trade at all**, but instead observes both agents, compares their decisions and learns from their successes and mistakes.

That way you’re not only comparing Atlas vs. Maverick — you’re also building a meta-layer that can potentially learn which type of behaviour works best under different market conditions.

I’d be very curious to see how their behaviour starts to diverge after a few weeks.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
drawdown matters more than return here, and I'd add time in the market. an aggressive mandate wins any month the market goes up just by being more exposed, so without exposure next to the return you mostly learn which way the market went.

I'd also log the reason each agent gives before every trade. the interesting stuff is usually where the stated reason and the actual trade don't match.

disclosure, I'm the one who built Quantradin. it runs agents like Atlas and Maverick next to each other on paper money at no cost, so a third mandate could get tried there before it gets real funding. quantradin.com if Maverick ever needs a sparring partner.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Starting both on the same capital with written mandates is a good setup. I'd add a plain benchmark (SPY or a 60/40 mix) and a fixed review period set in advance, because two agents over a few weeks will mostly show luck. Also track costs and slippage, how often each deviates from its mandate, and the number of trades behind each result. Writing down what would count as failure before you start helps too. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source you could use to see how each agent behaves around scheduled news.
